evidence_notes: Claim: limiting car usage is advantageous because environmental harm outweighs convenience. Support: three source articles used in one long body block -- 'In German Suburb, Life Goes On Without Cars' (12% of European greenhouse emissions, nearly 50% in congested US cities), 'Paris Bans Driving Due to Smog' (smog rivaling Beijing, reduced once driving limited), and a quoted line from 'The End of Car Culture' (transportation is America's second largest emissions source). Each is glossed, but the glosses mostly re-say the source ('This proves that cars can be a huge problem'). ORG 4 (controlling idea stated early and held, opening poses the convenience objection and a closing closes, every part relates; rung 5 fails -- the three source examples are interchangeable instances of one point and could swap in any order). DEV 4 (support specific throughout and the connection is stated for each piece -- 'These figures show that the reduction of car usage is pivotal'; rung 5 fails because the explanations restate the evidence rather than add interpretive work). CONV 3 (dense accumulation of misspellings -- conveinient, prevelant, knowldge, grenhouse, environemnt, neccesary, defnitly -- and one broken sentence, 'Cars produce so much pollution, have a gradual decuction in use would have possitive effects'; meaning always recoverable but rung 4 fails, the reader re-reads to repair). ARG 4 (rung 4 met: the convenience objection is raised in the opening and answered by an outweighing claim, and the emissions-share reason is reasoned toward the position; rung 5 fails on (d) -- the conclusion that limiting cars is advantageous is exactly what the prompt's framing implies, and the outweighing is asserted rather than argued).

Claim: the Face on Mars is a natural landform, not an alien construction. Support: one piece only -- the comparison to a butte in the Snake River Plain (misattributed to Ohio), with the reason that both are 'around the exact same height' and so 'therefore believed to be created in the same and natural way.' Everything else (aliens believed it, discovered 25 years ago, most NASA scientists believe it natural) is reported background, unsupported. ORG 3 (a controlling idea is present but weakly located -- it surfaces only at the end of a first paragraph that says the same thing three times in different words -- and the closing paragraph repeats the body without adding to it, so rung 4's 'held with a frame that works' fails on repetition rather than absence). DEV 3 (rung 3 met: the Butte/lava-dome comparison is a named specific; rung 4 fails -- the connection offered is circular, same height therefore same and natural way, so the reader still supplies why morphological similarity implies natural origin, and most claims go unsupported). CONV 3 (scientisis, Alian, discivered, reasonal, explination, abd, prooving; sentences run to one long 'scientists believe that X because Y' pattern and sprawl in the last paragraph; errors accumulate and force re-reading but never guessing). ARG 3 (rung 3 met -- the writer does commit, 'there is logical information prooving that this was a natural formation'; rung 4 fails, the reasoning is asserted through reported belief and the essay circles, with the final paragraph restating the opening in different words).

Claim: the author of 'The Challenge of Studying Venus' does not make a good case for exploring it. Support: quoted source lines -- corrosive sulfuric acid clouds, 'no spacecraft survived the landing for more than a few hours', 'the most Earth-like planet in our solar system', 800-degree surface temperatures, oceans that were 'probaly' once there -- with rhetorical questions doing the connecting. The one pro-exploration point is conceded then turned back: Venus was Earth-like but is now 'a destroyed Earth,' so the benefit no longer holds. ORG 5 (rung 5 met: the two body parts stand in a general-claim / concession relation -- 'the author is just making Venus sound like a horrible place' then 'the author does list at least one benefit' -- so they cannot swap without losing the concession; rung 6 fails, the closing lands nowhere the opening had not, and garbles itself, 'list the benefits to why we shouldnt explore Venus'). DEV 4 (support specific throughout and connections are stated -- 'You cant even walk on the surface without burning up, how is this like Earth?'; rung 5 fails, quotes are dropped alongside the writer's sentences and several are left to speak for themselves). CONV 3 (apostrophes absent throughout -- doesnt, cant, planets -- plus where/were and their/there confusions, lowercase i, questions punctuated as statements, tempatures, scientest, somone; errors accumulate and the reader repairs, notably 'list the benefits to why we shouldnt explore'). ARG 4 (rung 4 met: the opposing consideration is answered by showing it rests on a false assumption, past Earth-likeness is gone; rung 5 fails on (d) -- an evaluative verdict either way is what the prompt's framing already invites, and the essay gets no further than its own supporting reasons).

Claim: the emotion-reading classroom computer system 'might be help for some of the kids.' Support: two hypothetical scenarios -- students who get confused on a math problem but dislike raising their hand, and students at home who cannot ask the teacher except by email that may go unanswered. Neither is a realized instance; 'some kids i know' is gestured at but never made concrete. ORG 3 (rung 3 met, the controlling idea is stated in the first clause; rung 4 fails -- the text begins mid-argument with 'this new computer system' assumed known, offers no orientation, and the second unit starts on confusion and finishes on hand-raising reluctance before looping back). DEV 2 (rung 2 met, support is offered; rung 3 fails -- nothing is specific anywhere, no named case, no particular, no figure, only generic 'some kids' / 'the student' scenarios). CONV 2 (rung 3 fails: explame, webister, 'what id happening', 'try one some school', 'a mth problem' force outright guessing, not repair; no capitalization, whole essay is three run-on sentences, but meaning is broadly recoverable so rung 2 holds). ARG 4 (rung 4 met -- one reason is genuinely reasoned, not restated: the system helps because reluctant students need not raise a hand, and at home the teacher is unavailable, so the mechanism connecting reason to position is on the page; rung 5 fails, no opposing view, no principle, and the hedged 'good thing to try' conclusion is inside the prompt's framing).

Claim: cars marketed as driverless are not truly driverless, and the technology is worth pursuing as a human-machine partnership -- 'a team thing between technology and men.' Support: unnamed television shows the writer has watched ('every show that I have seen... has proved a big point'), the general assertion that today's driverless cars 'are fine,' and the general concession that they are expensive and risky. No named case, figure or instance anywhere. ORG 3 (rung 3 met -- a controlling idea is stated, but buried mid-body; rung 4 fails, the opening states something different and self-contradicting, 'driverless cars arent driverless cars,' and the television-show passage is a digression that does not bear on the position). DEV 2 (rung 2 met, support is offered; rung 3 fails -- support is general throughout, the TV shows are never named and never say what they showed). CONV 2 (rung 3 fails: 'driverless carsarent driverless cars' and 'were we would we learn the safety of our vehicles' both require guessing rather than repair; plus togther, remeber, completly, missing apostrophes throughout and frequent comma splices; meaning mostly recoverable so rung 2 holds). ARG 3 (rung 3 met, a position is stated and committed to at the close, 'its really worth it'; rung 4 fails -- the reasons are asserted, the human-oversight point sits awkwardly against the endorsement, and 'no one is perfect, we have to learn somewhere' restates rather than reasons).

Claim: emotion-reading software is something 'we humans should be happy to have.' Support: source detail used throughout -- Huang's claim that the system would modify the lesson for each person, 44 major facial muscles, the six basic emotions, raised eyebrows signalling surprise, and the Mona Lisa reading of 83% happy, 9% disgusted, 6% fearful, 2% angry, which is deployed against the skeptic. ORG 3 (rung 3 met, the controlling idea is stated in paragraph 2; rung 4 fails -- the position is not stated early, the one-sentence Huang paragraph on non-verbal communication is a digression that repeats itself inside itself, and the closing drifts off the position, 'currently this is just a project'). DEV 4 (support specific and connections stated in places -- the Mona Lisa figures answer the doubt, and boredom-detection is tied to modifying the lesson; rung 5 fails, the long 'what is the Facial Action Coding System' section reports the source with no connection stated). CONV 3 (garbled constructions requiring repair -- 'which would make it would modify the lesson', 'The machine can do so by it can tell', 'when the muscles around your lips it shows anger' -- plus simliar, surpise, benificial, somebodies, and questions punctuated as statements; errors accumulate, the reader re-reads but never guesses). ARG 4 (rung 4 met and the skeptic is acknowledged and answered with the Mona Lisa evidence and the improvability argument; rung 5 fails on (d) -- the conclusion is what the prompt's framing implies and the closing actually retreats from the position).

Claim, arrived at only by narration: the Face is a Martian mesa and believers 'have all been fooled.' Support: a chronological retelling of the source -- Viking 1's 1976 image, NASA's release, the face as pop icon in film, magazines and checkout lines, Mars Global Surveyor's arrival September 1997, the April 5 1998 MOC image 'ten times better' than Viking's, wispy clouds compromising it, and the April 2001 second look. Highly specific, but reported rather than put to work. ORG 3 (rung 3 met, the controlling idea is stated in the final sentence; rung 4 fails -- it is not stated early, the opening is a personal hook that never orients to the question, the pop-icon paragraph does not bear on natural-versus-alien, and the last paragraph stops rather than closes). DEV 3 (rung 3 met with abundant named specifics; rung 4 fails -- the details are narrated in sequence and the reader supplies what each shows, with some source phrasing carried over unmarked, 'bona fide evidence of life on mars', 'Martian equivalent to a butte or mesa'). CONV 3 (Propulison, suprised, aound, apppeared, sotre, ofr, 'went ot', 'flow over', '200l', missing spaces after periods, one sentence that never resolves -- 'As NASA's Viking 1 spacecraft was circling aound Mars and found a figure similar to a human face, believe me when i say it'; errors accumulate and force re-reading, but meaning stays recoverable). ARG 3 (rung 3 met, the closing commits; rung 4 fails -- the essay narrates events rather than reasoning from them, the alien view is waved off as 'there own opinion' rather than engaged, and no why is stated for why the later images settle the question).

Claim: citizens' votes, not electors' votes, should decide the presidency. Support: two properly attributed source quotations -- Posner's 'when you vote for a presidential candidate you're actually voting for a slate of electors' and Plumer's 'can voters control whom their electors vote for? Not always' -- each followed by a gloss. Surrounding generalizations (most presidents make no difference, candidates' intentions are harmful, 'Society will be living in hell') carry no support. ORG 3 (rung 3 met, the controlling idea closes paragraph 1 after an opening that wanders through presidential duties and mistakes; rung 4 fails -- there is no closing at all, the essay breaks off at 'furthermore,'). DEV 4 (support is specific and the connection is stated for both quotes -- 'what the author clearly states is...', 'this quote shows that...'; rung 5 fails because both glosses restate the quotation in other words rather than adding to it, and several sweeping claims go entirely unsupported). CONV 3 (presidnets, duites, couted, Somtimes, priveliges, lifes, want's, sentence-initial lowercase throughout, comma splices, and one sentence needing repair -- 'Presidents sometimes do not compensate for the mistakes they make that they're not supposed to make'; errors accumulate, reader re-reads). ARG 4 (rung 4 met -- the why is on the page: because the vote goes to a slate of electors whom voters cannot control, citizens get outcomes they did not choose and suffer for four years; rung 5 fails on (d), the abolish conclusion is exactly what the prompt's framing offers, and Posner's defense is quoted without being engaged).

Claim: the reader should join the Seagoing Cowboys program, written in the persona of a participant. Support: three enumerated reasons with concrete source-derived detail -- caring for animals (horses, young cows and mules; one cargo of 335 horses plus hay and oats), games (baseball, volleyball, table-tennis, fencing, boxing, whittling, played in empty holds), and duties (watchman shifts, hourly animal checks, hourly report to the captain), plus travel to Greece, Crete, the Panama Canal and China. ORG 4 (controlling idea stated early, opening and closing both present, all three reasons relate; rung 5 fails -- the animals and games paragraphs are interchangeable, the ordering is announced rather than motivated, and only the third is marked 'most important'). DEV 4 (support is specific throughout, including a figure, and connections are stated in places -- 'These games helped us pass time when we didnt have work to do'; rung 5 fails, most pieces are listed and closed with assertion, 'it will be all worth it in the end', and some phrasing is carried in from the source unmarked though it sits inside the writer's own sentences). CONV 3 ('It's every fun', 'take care animals', vist, oversea, 'you will to', comma splices, and one sentence needing repair -- 'especially on when I returned from trips and the animals had been unloaded'; errors accumulate, reader re-reads). ARG 3 (rung 3 met, the position is clear and held; rung 4 fails -- the reasons reduce to 'it was fun', and the closing inference, 'if i had fun being one then I feel like you will to', asserts transfer rather than reasoning it, so the essay circles its opening).

Claim: driverless cars would be beneficial, reducing driver-caused accidents. Support: three quotations from the source, one with a paragraph citation -- paragraph 7 on cars notifying the driver when the road 'requires human skills', 'Automakers are continuing their work on the assumption that the problems ahead will be solved', and 'Mercedes-Benz, Audi, and Nissan plan to have cars that can drive themselves by 2020'. ORG 4 (controlling idea stated early and held, opening orients and a closing closes, both body parts relate; rung 5 fails -- the two body paragraphs are the same objection-then-answer shape and could swap without loss). DEV 4 (support specific and each piece has a stated connection; rung 5 fails because the key gloss, 'This leads me to believe that these cars are safe', declares the conclusion without saying how the handoff feature produces safety). CONV 4 (benefical, potentally, imporvements, 'cars sensors' without an apostrophe, and two fragments punctuated as sentences -- 'Such as figuring out who is at fault...' and 'Which means that chances are...'; errors are visible and control wobbles at those two points, but nothing needs repair and the reader never re-reads, so rung 5's 'stays under control at every length' is what fails). ARG 4 (rung 4 met -- the danger objection is acknowledged and answered by the driver-remains-alert design; rung 5 fails on (d), the conclusion is inside the prompt's framing, the liability objection is answered only by deferring to automakers' assumption, and the close swaps the evaluative question for inevitability).
